network.target_molecule: Arginine, stereochemically unspecified; racemic product expected
network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, atom-balanced hypothesis network, not a demonstrated complete prebiotic synthesis. Ten distinct reaction-node sequences are obtained by combining five proposed scaffold-construction branches with two chemically different endgames: aminonitrile hydrolysis and hydantoin formation followed by hydrolysis. These are not ten independently established prebiotic routes. The supplied review does not provide sufficient reaction-level evidence to establish even one complete arginine synthesis under a compatible geochemical sequence. Its three cyclization variants are therefore not counted as separate pathways, its oxygen-free formation of an oxygenated intermediate is rejected, and no L-selectivity is claimed. The review-inspired branch retains early guanidination but explicitly identifies its reductive bottlenecks. Alternative succinonitrile branches bypass both hydroxythioamide deoxygenation and thioamide-to-aldehyde conversion; their different selectivity problems are also identified. Sulfite-to-sulfate bookkeeping supplies explicit reducing equivalents without incorrectly treating regenerated H2S as a net reductant. Sulfate formation and productive substrate reduction nevertheless require experimental confirmation. Copper-catalyzed hydrocyanation, sulfide addition, and irradiation are separate operations, not an assumed compatible one-pot mixture. Every numerical condition below is a prospective screening window, not a reported arginine experiment or an established natural operating window. Hydrothermal branches require shallow geothermal circulation connected to surface pools; transport, reconcentration, catalyst separation, and intermediate survival remain unvalidated. Organic structures use neutral reference forms, with aqueous protonation equilibria omitted. Null environment_formed values identify external feedstocks or, for mol_022 and mol_027, formation in more than one environment.

reactions.name: Copper(I)-assisted acetylene hydrocyanation

conditions.other: Prospective sulfide-free gas-water contact stage; mildly acidic chloride-bearing water; screen 0.1-10 mM dissolved copper. Copper speciation, gas delivery, and polymerization losses require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-assisted addition of HCN across the acetylene triple bond forms the vinyl nitrile. This is hydrocyanation, not an uncatalyzed Michael addition to an electrophilic acetylene carbon.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review attributes this entry reaction to Patel et al. (2015). Copper(I) catalysis is chemically more defensible than the review's bare nucleophilic-addition description. The stated conditions are screening assumptions, not verified conditions from that paper. Sulfide must not be assumed compatible with the dissolved copper catalyst because copper sulfide precipitation can remove it.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8.5-10; ammonia in excess over acrylonitrile; shaded or nighttime reaction period; screen hours to days.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds at the beta carbon of acrylonitrile, followed by proton transfer to form 3-aminopropanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This reaction class and substrate pair are included in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) summary. Excess ammonia is intended to favor monoaddition, but additional cyanoethylation, polymerization, and ammonia volatilization must be quantified. No selective yield is inferred from the network.

reactions.name: Early guanidination of 3-aminopropanenitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8-10; concentrated aqueous phase with cyanamide in excess; screen 1-7 days; avoid complete drying and sustained UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: The primary amine attacks the nitrile carbon of cyanamide; proton transfers generate the substituted guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review assigns this transformation to Patel et al. (2015), but does not provide its yield or operating window. Early guanidination avoids having to distinguish the alpha and side-chain amino groups of ornithine later. Cyanamide hydrolysis, oligomerization, and subsequent cyclization of the product remain competing reactions.

reactions.name: Guanidine formation from cyanamide and ammonia

conditions.other: Prospective concentrated ammoniacal solution, pH 9-11; screen days to weeks. Evaporation must be balanced against ammonia loss.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to cyanamide, followed by proton transfer to give guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as an effective prebiotic supply reaction under these conditions; it is not established by the supplied Patel et al. (2015) material. The transformation is chemically motivated by cyanamide's electrophilic carbon, but ammonia is a weaker nucleophile than many alkylamines. Cyanamide dimerization and hydrolysis may dominate.

reactions.name: Guanidine conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Prospective concentrated solution at pH 10-11; screen 1-7 days. Measure the unprotonated guanidine fraction and cyclic products rather than assuming productive conversion.

reactions.mechanism: An unprotonated guanidine nitrogen undergoes aza-Michael addition to acrylonitrile, followed by proton transfer.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative alternative to rxn_002 plus rxn_003; no substrate-specific support is supplied by Patel et al. (2015). It reverses the order of guanidine assembly and carbon-chain attachment without introducing an aminoaldehyde. Guanidine protonation strongly limits nucleophilicity, and intramolecular capture of the remaining nitrile could prevent accumulation of the required open-chain product.

reactions.name: Proposed partial reduction of guanidino propanenitrile to an aldehyde

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9, substrate 1-10 mM, sulfite 10-100 mM, ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM; screen 1-24 hours. A 254 nm source at 1-10 W/m2 is a laboratory proxy, not an asserted early-Earth spectrum. Exclude added sulfide and dissolved copper.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized two-electron reduction of the nitrile to an imine followed by hydrolysis. The balanced net reaction consumes two waters and oxidizes sulfite to sulfate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific reduction. Patel et al. (2015) provides the supplied cyanosulfidic context, while Xu et al. (2018) supports sulfite/ferrocyanide photoredox homologation for other substrates, not this guanidino nitrile. This formulation supplies explicit reducing equivalents instead of treating nitrile-to-hemiaminal conversion as simple hydrolysis. Selective aldehyde production, guanidine survival, mediator turnover, and sulfate versus other sulfur products must all be demonstrated.

reactions.name: Reversible formation of the six-membered guanidine hemiaminal

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9; shaded equilibration after irradiation. Determine the open-chain aldehyde fraction and competing condensation products.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular addition of a guanidine nitrogen to the aldehyde forms a six-membered cyclic hemiaminal without net addition or loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: This is a chemically corrected, speculative interpretation of the cyclic intermediate described in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) review. It distinguishes genuine hemiaminal formation from nitrile reduction and does not count omitted water or ammonia as alternative pathways. Productive downstream chemistry requires a measurable equilibrium population of the open-chain aldehyde.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin trapping of the cyclic-hemiaminal equilibrium

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8-9 and total cyanide 10-100 mM; shaded reaction interval. Monitor HCN escape, cyanohydrin reversal, and ring-opening equilibrium.

reactions.mechanism: The cyclic hemiaminal reversibly opens to its aldehyde; cyanide adds to that carbonyl and protonation gives the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review associates this conversion with Patel et al. (2015). The aldehyde-trapping mechanism is more defensible than direct cyanide displacement at a saturated hemiaminal carbon with unexplained retention of hydroxyl. Substrate-specific equilibrium constants and selectivity are missing, so productive trapping remains a hypothesis rather than an established step.

reactions.name: Hydrogen sulfide addition to the cyanohydrin nitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9 and dissolved sulfide 10-100 mM; screen hours to days in a copper-depleted, shaded solution.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide attacks the nitrile carbon; proton transfer and tautomerization yield the thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: This reaction is included in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) summary and is consistent with known nitrile thiolysis chemistry. H2S is a stoichiometric sulfur reagent here, not an unspecified catalyst. The guanidino substrate's yield and competition with cyanohydrin dissociation are not established by the supplied information.

reactions.name: Proposed sulfite-driven reductive deoxygenation of the hydroxythioamide

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9; sulfite 10-100 mM and ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM; laboratory 254 nm irradiation for 1-24 hours. Residual sulfide from rxn_009 must be measured and reduced before testing rather than assumed harmless.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed two-electron reductive replacement of the alpha hydroxyl group by hydrogen. Sulfite oxidation provides the reducing equivalents; water cancels from the balanced net equation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a decisive bottleneck, not a demonstrated repair of the review's Cu/H2S step. Patel et al. (2015), as summarized, motivates deoxygenation; Xu et al. (2018) motivates testing an explicit sulfite photoredox donor but does not establish this transformation. C-O cleavage must outcompete thioamide reduction, fragmentation, and photolysis. Sulfate production and carbon-product selectivity must be measured independently. This step does not homologate the carbon skeleton.

reactions.name: Proposed reductive hydrolysis of the guanidino thioamide

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9, sulfite 10-100 mM, ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM; screen short irradiation intervals up to 24 hours. Quantify accumulating H2S, aldehyde trapping efficiency, and competing amide or amine formation.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized two-electron reduction and hydrolytic cleavage of the thioamide to aldehyde, ammonia, and hydrogen sulfide. Two waters are consumed in the balanced net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a second decisive bottleneck. The supplied Patel et al. (2015) review compresses a redox-demanding conversion into a thioamide-to-cyanohydrin exchange. Here sulfite, not sulfur already present in the substrate, is explicitly oxidized as the external donor. This fixes bookkeeping but does not establish a productive mechanism. Aldehyde selectivity, sulfur fate, sulfide inhibition, and photocatalyst turnover remain unresolved; pathways P5-P10 bypass this reaction entirely.

reactions.name: Conjugate hydrocyanation of acrylonitrile to succinonitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8.5-10; concentrated cyanide-containing water; screen hours to days. Quantify polymerization and HCN loss.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide undergoes conjugate addition to acrylonitrile, followed by protonation to form succinonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a geochemical supply step in this network, although conjugate hydrocyanation is established reaction-class chemistry. The supplied Patel et al. (2015) material supports considering acrylonitrile as an intermediate but does not document this branch. It creates the required four-carbon backbone without the hydroxythioamide deoxygenation sequence and is included for that chemical advantage, not merely for pathway count.

reactions.name: Proposed selective monohydrogenation of succinonitrile
agents: Fresh native nickel-rich iron-nickel alloy surface

conditions.pressure: 10-100 bar total; prospective hydrogen partial pressure 1-20 bar
conditions.other: Prospective sulfide-poor geothermal pores, pH 8-10, excess ammonia, and 1-24 hour contact. Test low conversion, catalyst passivation, product cyclization, and overhydrogenation. Subsequent cooling and transport to a surface capture stage are required but not demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen activation on nickel followed by hydrogenation of one nitrile group to a primary amine; two H2 molecules are required.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no substrate-selective hydrothermal experiment is supplied. Nickel is justified by its ability to activate hydrogen and catalyze nitrile hydrogenation, not by mineral availability alone. The principal problems are reduction of both nitriles, five-membered cyclic amidine formation from 4-aminobutanenitrile, and alloy sulfidation. Neither excess ammonia nor low conversion is assumed to solve these problems. This route is unacceptable as a productive pathway unless recoverable mono-reduced product is demonstrated.

reactions.name: Guanidination of 4-aminobutanenitrile before aldehyde generation

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8-10, cyanamide in excess, and 1-72 hour reaction time. Hydrothermal feed, if used, must first cool and lose contact with the hydrogenation catalyst. Transport and capture times must be compared with measured cyclization kinetics.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal primary amine adds to cyanamide to form the guanidino nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative extension of the amine guanidination summarized for Patel et al. (2015). It avoids late, nonselective guanidination of ornithine and avoids making unprotected 4-aminobutanal. However, 4-aminobutanenitrile can cyclize before guanidination. No pH or residence-time window is known from the supplied evidence in which useful guanidination outcompetes that reaction.

reactions.name: Proposed partial photoreduction of succinonitrile to a cyanoaldehyde

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9, succinonitrile 1-10 mM, sulfite 10-100 mM, ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM; screen brief irradiation intervals within 1-24 hours. Avoid added HCN during aldehyde generation.

reactions.mechanism: Two-electron reduction of one nitrile to an imine followed by hydrolysis gives 3-cyanopropanal. Two waters are consumed in the net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific extrapolation from the photoredox reaction class discussed by Patel et al. (2015) and Xu et al. (2018). The equivalent nitrile groups do not provide intrinsic protection against double reduction. Productive aldehyde capture must outcompete further reduction, hydration, and oligomerization. Unlike an aminoaldehyde route, this intermediate cannot directly form the problematic five-membered imine of 4-aminobutanal.

reactions.name: Proposed reductive amination of the cyanoaldehyde

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8-10, ammonia in substantial excess, sulfite 10-100 mM, and ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM. Exclude added cyanide during imine formation and screen short irradiation periods.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or iminium species with the aldehyde; reduction gives the amino nitrile. Water from condensation cancels water used in the formal sulfite oxidation half-reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; the supplied Patel et al. (2015) research does not establish this reductive amination. It offers a surface alternative to hydrothermal nitrile hydrogenation, not a proven selectivity improvement. Reduction of the carbonyl to an alcohol, reduction of the remaining nitrile, and cyclization of the amino-nitrile product may dominate. Productive imine reduction and subsequent guanidination require direct testing.

reactions.name: Proposed reductive alkylation of guanidine with the cyanoaldehyde

conditions.other: Prospective pH 9.5-11, guanidine in excess, sulfite 10-100 mM, and ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM. Determine whether any condensable guanidine fraction exists before applying photoreduction.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized condensation of an unprotonated guanidine nitrogen with the aldehyde followed by reduction of the resulting C=N linkage.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and the least-supported scaffold-entry branch; no supporting substrate experiment is supplied by Patel et al. (2015). Its chemical purpose is to bypass both the aminoaldehyde problem and cyclization of free 4-aminobutanenitrile. Strong guanidine protonation, weak condensation, and competing carbonyl reduction may make it ineffective. Inclusion denotes a falsifiable alternative, not evidence that reductive guanidine alkylation works prebiotically.

reactions.name: Proposed partial reduction of the guanidino butanenitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 7-9, substrate 1-10 mM, sulfite 10-100 mM, ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM, and 1-24 hour irradiation screen. Stop irradiation before attempting Strecker capture.

reactions.mechanism: Two-electron nitrile reduction followed by imine hydrolysis gives 4-guanidinobutanal, ammonia, and sulfate; two waters are consumed.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific application of the photoredox class discussed by Patel et al. (2015) and Xu et al. (2018). This branch avoids the two thioamide bottlenecks but introduces a different selective nitrile-reduction requirement. Guanidine survival, aldehyde overreduction, and possible seven-membered cyclic-hemiaminal formation must be measured. A persistent, freely available aldehyde is not assumed.

reactions.name: Strecker formation of arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 8-9, aldehyde 1-10 mM, total cyanide 10-100 mM, and ammonia in excess; shaded reaction interval of hours to days. Redox mediators and sulfide carryover must be assessed.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible aldehyde-ammonia condensation forms an imine or iminium species, followed by cyanide addition to produce the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied Patel et al. (2015) review places an aminonitrile immediately before arginine. This mechanism corrects its description of ammonia simply displacing an unactivated hydroxyl group: cyanohydrin and aminonitrile products can communicate through aldehyde/imine equilibria. The reaction class is established, but this substrate's yield and accessible aldehyde fraction are not. Achiral reagents provide no basis for an L-only product.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted hydration of arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Prospective pH 0-1 in a concentrated acidic geothermal pool; screen 1-30 days. Such acidity is an environmental requirement to establish, not a consequence of the Surface label. Assess cyanide and iron-cyanide carryover before acidification.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation and water addition produce an imidic intermediate that tautomerizes to argininamide.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied Patel et al. (2015) review invokes nitrile hydrolysis but gives no numerical conditions or intermediate yields. Separating hydration from amide cleavage exposes a possible kinetic bottleneck. The proposed acidic window is not a literature-derived arginine result; slower natural conditions may be inadequate, and decomposition can compete with hydration.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted hydrolysis of argininamide to arginine

conditions.other: Prospective pH 0-1 and 1-30 day screening period. Measure both amide disappearance and intact arginine formation; cool the product-containing solution after reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed water addition to the amide carbonyl followed by C-N cleavage gives the amino acid and ammonia, present mainly as ammonium under these conditions.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the conventional hydrolysis sequence invoked in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) review. The reaction family is credible, but complete selective conversion in an actual prebiotic pool is not established by that citation. Strong-acid availability, residence time, guanidino-group preservation, and cumulative losses remain necessary tests. The product is stereochemically unspecified arginine.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs-type trapping of arginine aminonitrile as a hydantoin

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar; prospective CO2 partial pressure 0.01-0.1 bar
conditions.other: Prospective ammonium-carbonate-containing solution at pH 8-9.5; screen 1-7 days. Determine carbonate speciation and competition between alpha-amino and guanidino interactions with CO2.

reactions.mechanism: CO2 capture by the alpha-amino group, cyclization involving the nitrile, and rearrangement give the hydantoin. The net transformation incorporates one CO2 without net water consumption.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific extension of Bucherer-Bergs chemistry; this branch is not demonstrated in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) material. It is a genuinely different endgame from direct nitrile hydration, not an alternative stoichiometric rendering of the same step. Guanidinium-carbonate association, competing nitrogen-site chemistry, and hydantoin yield are unresolved.

reactions.name: Warm alkaline opening of arginine hydantoin

conditions.other: Prospective pH 10-11 and residence times of 1-30 days in recirculating geothermal pores. Requires infiltration of a concentrated surface product and retention against dilution; neither transport efficiency nor lifetime is known.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-assisted attack at the hydantoin carbonyl opens the ring to an N-carbamoyl amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this guanidino hydantoin and this geochemical window; no supporting experiment is supplied by Patel et al. (2015). Warmer pressurized water addresses the known kinetic difficulty of hydantoin hydrolysis, but does not establish adequate rates at pH 10-11. Adsorption, dilution, and thermal destruction must be included in any feasibility assessment.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic decarbamoylation to arginine

conditions.other: Prospective pH 10-11 and 1-30 day screening interval, followed by cooling. Compare selective alpha-decarbamoylation with guanidino-group degradation and amino-acid destruction.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the alpha-ureido group releases arginine, ammonia, and inorganic carbon, represented by CO2 in the net equation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a major endpoint bottleneck. Neither the supplied Patel et al. (2015) material nor the existence of a hydantoin intermediate establishes selective nonenzymatic decarbamoylation here. Stronger laboratory conditions might be needed than the proposed geothermal window can supply. Productive arginine accumulation cannot be claimed unless this reaction outruns side-chain hydrolysis and thermal degradation.

pathways.name: Early aminonitrile guanidination with direct amino-acid hydrolysis
pathways.description: Review-inspired scaffold construction followed by Strecker chemistry and stepwise aminonitrile hydrolysis. Conditional on selective rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_011; the latter two remain unvalidated decisive bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Early aminonitrile guanidination with hydantoin capture
pathways.description: Uses the P1 scaffold branch but diverts the final aminonitrile through a hydantoin. It does not solve the scaffold-reduction bottlenecks and additionally requires demonstrated transport and selective warm hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Guanidine-first conjugate addition with direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Forms guanidine before attaching it to acrylonitrile. Distinct from P1 in bond-construction order, but more uncertain because productive guanidine addition must compete with protonation and cyclization. Shares the review-inspired reductive bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Guanidine-first conjugate addition with hydantoin capture
pathways.description: Combines the guanidine-first scaffold branch with the hydantoin endgame. This is a formal candidate route, not independent evidence for either upstream guanidine addition or downstream hydantoin hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Succinonitrile monohydrogenation with direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Builds the four-carbon backbone by conjugate hydrocyanation, hydrogenates one nitrile, and guanidinates before generating an aldehyde. Bypasses both thioamide bottlenecks and avoids unprotected 4-aminobutanal. Selective monohydrogenation, amino-nitrile cyclization, transfer, and rxn_018 remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Succinonitrile monohydrogenation with hydantoin capture
pathways.description: Uses the thioamide-free P5 scaffold branch and the hydantoin endgame. Requires demonstrated surface-to-geothermal and geothermal-to-surface material handling, rather than an assumed unspecified ocean-to-land transfer.

pathways.name: Cyanoaldehyde reductive amination with direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Uses surface photoreduction and reductive amination instead of hydrothermal nitrile hydrogenation. Bypasses the thioamide sequence but requires selective single-nitrile reduction, imine reduction, and guanidination before amino-nitrile cyclization.

pathways.name: Cyanoaldehyde reductive amination with hydantoin capture
pathways.description: Combines the surface cyanoaldehyde/reductive-amination scaffold branch with hydantoin formation and warm hydrolysis. The hydantoin branch is not assumed to compensate for poor scaffold yield or unstable amino-nitrile intermediates.

pathways.name: Direct reductive guanidine alkylation with direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Attaches preformed guanidine to a cyanoaldehyde before reducing the remaining nitrile. Avoids both unprotected aminoaldehydes and free 4-aminobutanenitrile, but depends on the especially uncertain guanidine condensation/reduction step rxn_017.

pathways.name: Direct reductive guanidine alkylation with hydantoin capture
pathways.description: Pairs the most speculative scaffold-entry branch with the alternative hydantoin endgame. It is included as an explicitly conditional experimental hypothesis, not a validated tenth prebiotic synthesis.

evaluation.target_molecule: Arginine, stereochemically unspecified; racemic product expected

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon-skeleton construction and final aminonitrile hydrolysis form a formally coherent route to racemic arginine. However, rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_011 remain major chemical bottlenecks. Sulfite-to-sulfate bookkeeping supplies the correct formal reducing equivalents but does not establish selective nitrile reduction, hydroxythioamide deoxygenation, or thioamide-to-aldehyde conversion. Cyanohydrin trapping through an aldehyde/hemiaminal equilibrium is more defensible than assuming direct substitution at the cyclic hemiaminal. Productive flux through that equilibrium remains unmeasured.
suggestions: Demonstrate rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_011 on the specified guanidino substrates, identifying competing hydrolysis, hydrogenation, and sulfur-containing products.
Measure both organic product yields and sulfur oxidation products; sulfate formation alone would not demonstrate productive substrate reduction.
Specify irradiation, pH, temperature, residence time, and intermediate survival through the transition to acid hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway inherits the unresolved scaffold reductions of P1. Hydantoin formation from an aminonitrile and CO2 is a recognized reaction class, but its operation with this guanidino substrate is not established by the supplied evidence. Hydantoin opening and subsequent decarbamoylation are distinct kinetic requirements: warm alkaline conditions do not by themselves establish efficient completion of both. More forcing hydrolysis could also damage the guanidino side chain. Shallow geothermal circulation is a conceivable transport setting, but delivery, dilution, and intermediate survival are not demonstrated.
suggestions: Resolve the upstream reductive bottlenecks before treating hydantoin capture as a complete alternative endgame.
Establish substrate-specific hydantoin formation, ring-opening, and decarbamoylation rates, including guanidino-group retention.
Define geothermal fluid composition and residence times and measure recovery after the proposed transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The guanidine-first branch reaches the same correctly identified scaffold as P1, but guanidine production and selective conjugate addition require better condition support. Guanidinium predominance at most aqueous pH values makes the nucleophilicity and selectivity assumed in rxn_005 condition-dependent; cyanamide conversion in rxn_004 also competes with hydrolysis and oligomerization. Neither upstream alternative resolves the decisive uncertainties in rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_011. The final acid hydrolysis is chemically credible if the aminonitrile can first be obtained.
suggestions: Determine guanidine yield from cyanamide and ammonia under explicit aqueous or wet-dry conditions.
Measure guanidine/acrylonitrile monoaddition selectivity as a function of protonation state and competing cyclization.
Demonstrate the three reductive transformations independently and then in a connected material-transfer sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The molecular connectivity is coherent, but the pathway combines uncertain guanidine-first chemistry, three poorly supported scaffold reductions, and an unvalidated hydantoin hydrolysis sequence. The principal problem is not the number or order of environments: it is the absence of demonstrated productive chemistry and intermediate survival under specified conditions. In particular, selective nonenzymatic decarbamoylation cannot be inferred from hydantoin ring opening.
suggestions: Provide separate evidence for guanidine formation, conjugate addition, and the proposed sulfite-mediated reductions.
Test the hydantoin endgame with an independently characterized arginine aminonitrile sample.
Quantify arginine production versus accumulation of N-alpha-carbamoylarginine and degradation of the guanidino group.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest conditional candidate because it replaces the especially uncertain hydroxythioamide deoxygenation and thioamide-to-aldehyde chemistry with a recognized nitrile hydrogenation reaction class. Nevertheless, rxn_013 does not specify an active catalyst, hydrogen pressure, or conditions that favor reduction of only one nitrile. Further hydrogenation and cyclization of gamma-aminobutyronitrile to a five-membered amidine are important competing outcomes. Guanidination must outcompete those reactions, and rxn_018 still lacks substrate-specific evidence for selective aldehyde production. The Strecker and acid-hydrolysis endgame is credible but conditional on obtaining mol_020.
suggestions: Identify a geochemically credible hydrogenation catalyst and demonstrate the yield of gamma-aminobutyronitrile relative to diamine and cyclic products.
Establish whether the aminonitrile survives transport and can be guanidinated before cyclization or further reaction.
Validate rxn_018 and immediate aldehyde capture while monitoring overreduction, sulfite adduct formation, and intramolecular guanidine capture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The scaffold strategy avoids the thioamide bottlenecks but retains the unresolved selectivity of succinonitrile monohydrogenation and guanidino-nitrile partial reduction. Hydantoin capture could provide a useful intermediate, but no stability or recovery advantage is demonstrated. Completion of rxn_024 under conditions that preserve arginine is less secure than the direct acid-hydrolysis endgame. The proposed circulation must also preserve the reactive aminonitrile during its first transfer and the hydantoin during subsequent processing.
suggestions: Resolve hydrogenation selectivity and identify the catalyst before assigning a viable hydrothermal operating window.
Measure whether hydantoin capture actually improves storage stability or recovery.
Demonstrate complete chemical hydrolysis to arginine, rather than only ring opening to the carbamoylated intermediate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanoaldehyde route is structurally coherent and avoids the thioamide transformations. Its feasibility instead depends on selective reduction of one succinonitrile group, reductive amination without reducing the remaining nitrile or aldehyde to unwanted products, and another selective nitrile-to-aldehyde conversion. Sulfite can participate in photoredox chemistry, but the supplied material does not establish these particular transformations or their compatibility with aldehyde-bisulfite equilibria. The gamma-aminobutyronitrile cyclization problem remains. The final acid hydrolysis is plausible.
suggestions: Measure mono-reduction selectivity in rxn_015, including reduction of both nitriles and aldehyde overreduction.
Demonstrate productive reductive amination in rxn_016 while accounting for imine formation, sulfite adducts, and cyclic amidine products.
Specify the light spectrum, photon exposure, pH, and reagent carryover for each separate photochemical operation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines the unresolved selective photoreductions and reductive amination of P7 with an incompletely supported hydantoin endgame. All transformations conserve atoms and charge with the supplied coefficients, but that does not establish productive photochemistry or hydrolysis kinetics. Hydantoin formation is chemically plausible as a reaction class; selective release of arginine from N-alpha-carbamoylarginine remains a separate bottleneck. Surface-to-geothermal transfer is conceivable but lacks a quantified survival and dilution model.
suggestions: Validate the cyanoaldehyde and reductive-amination sequence with complete product analysis.
Determine whether residual sulfite, ammonia, or other upstream reagents interfere with hydantoin formation.
Measure hydantoin transport recovery and selective hydrolysis under a specified geothermal fluid composition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Direct reductive guanidine alkylation is the defining weakness. Guanidine cannot simply be assumed to behave like ammonia in an aqueous reductive amination: protonation, resonance-delocalized nucleophilicity, condensation equilibria, and alkylation selectivity require specific support. Sulfite oxidation alone does not establish reduction of the necessary condensed intermediate. The pathway also retains uncertain cyanoaldehyde generation and guanidino-nitrile partial reduction. Avoiding free gamma-aminobutyronitrile removes one possible cyclization problem, but does not validate rxn_017.
suggestions: Demonstrate formation and reduction of the proposed guanidine-aldehyde condensation intermediate under explicit aqueous conditions.
Identify the N-alkylated product structurally and quantify competing aldehyde reduction and multiple alkylation.
Establish selective cyanoaldehyde generation and subsequent nitrile reduction independently of the guanidine-alkylation hypothesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route is formally connected to arginine but combines poorly established direct guanidine reductive alkylation with selective nitrile photoreductions and an uncertain nonenzymatic decarbamoylation. Hydantoin capture does not resolve the upstream alkylation problem, and ring opening alone would leave the network at N-alpha-carbamoylarginine rather than the target. The proposed environmental separation is sensible as a hypothesis, but the necessary operating conditions and intermediate recoveries are not supplied.
suggestions: Prioritize experimental validation of rxn_017 before developing its downstream environmental sequence.
Establish hydantoin formation and complete hydrolysis with authenticated substrate and product standards.
Quantify guanidino-group survival, transport losses, and target accumulation under the actual proposed conditions.

evaluation.network_feedback: Not approved as a viable complete synthesis network on the supplied evidence. Network validity is strong: the 29 molecule nodes and 24 reaction nodes are connected, identifiers are consistent, and every pathway formally reaches the correct stereochemically unspecified arginine target. The deterministic check establishes 19 reactions balanced as written and five balanceable with ordinary coefficients; there are no conservation violations. The explicit equations should retain 2 H2O in rxn_006, rxn_011, rxn_015, and rxn_018, and 2 H2 in rxn_013. These coefficient requirements are not chemical defects. The principal limitations are selective substrate reduction and target-producing throughput. Review-inspired branches depend on rxn_006, rxn_010, and rxn_011; alternative branches avoid the thioamide bottlenecks but still require unvalidated selectivity in rxn_013 or rxn_015-rxn_017 and in rxn_018. All routes require productive generation and Strecker capture of 4-guanidinobutanal, whose competing intramolecular reactions also need evaluation. Direct aminonitrile hydrolysis is the better-supported endgame; hydantoin decarbamoylation adds a distinct unresolved kinetic and selectivity requirement. Environmental consistency cannot be established from Surface and Hydrothermal labels alone. Despite the introduction's reference to numerical screening windows, none are supplied in the reaction list. Temperature, pH, pressure, irradiation, residence time, catalyst speciation, and transfer recovery remain unspecified. Separating copper hydrocyanation, sulfide addition, and irradiation appropriately avoids asserting one-pot compatibility, but does not demonstrate catalyst removal or intermediate survival. Literature alignment is partial: the network appropriately rejects the review's oxygen-free oxygenation, avoids unsupported L-selectivity, and acknowledges that its ten sequences are not ten demonstrated syntheses. However, the supplied review's attribution of a complete arginine route to Patel et al. (2015), DOI 10.1038/nchem.2202, is not substantiated here by primary reaction-level procedures, yields, or product characterization. That citation cannot establish the substituted sulfite reductions, succinonitrile branches, or hydantoin endgame. No reaction-specific citations accompany the proposed reaction entries. P5 is the strongest conditional candidate because of the relative chemical plausibility of its transformations, not its step count, hub structure, feedstocks, or environmental ordering. Reaction scores describe conditional plausibility; the lower pathway and network confidences reflect unresolved bottlenecks in complete target production.
